A cloud backup to Google's servers — not a phone-to-USB copy.; Google Android Help, "Back up your phone" (Back up your phone - Android Help) — Settings > Google > All services > Backup, turn on Backup by Google One, tap Back up now. A cloud backup to Google's servers — not a phone-to-USB copy.; Cat S62 Pro vs Cat S75 specs (Cat S62 Pro vs Cat S75) — USB "Yes, USB-C v2.0" with USB features "USB on-the-go, USB Charging" for both models. A spec comparison, not a guide — and the confirmation that the S75 and the S62 Pro have OTG.; Cat S53 specs (Cat S53 - Full phone specifications) — "USB Type-C 3.0, OTG", microSDXC card slot using the shared SIM slot, 128 GB of storage, 6 GB RAM, 5,500 mAh battery. A spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the S53 has OTG.; Notebookcheck, "The CAT S62 Pro Rugged Smartphone Review" (The CAT S62 Pro Rugged Smartphone Review) — "Thanks to USB OTG functionality, users can connect peripheral devices to the CAT smartphone." A review, not a guide — and a second confirmation that the S62 Pro has OTG.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a CAT-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated CAT photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: A CAT phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the S75 and the S62 Pro list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, and the S53 lists USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the current models, while a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three CAT specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current rugged models — spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the S75 and the S62 Pro, and USB Type-C 3.0 with OTG for the S53. Second, CAT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the per-model backup guides all point to the same three things: connect the phone to a computer and copy the files, back up to Google Drive, or use Google Photos for photos — with a microSD card as the local option; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; CAT camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The S75 and the S53 both take a microSDXC card that uses the shared SIM slot (up to 512 GB on the S53), while the S62 Pro has a dedicated microSDXC slot — so a card is an option, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: CAT's own tools (Google backup, Google Photos, per-model FAQ guides — not phone-to-USB). If you want CAT's own route, know what each tool actually does — the per-model backup guides for the S75 all point to the same three things, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google backup is the first way the guides describe — Settings > Google > All services > Backup, "Backup by Google One" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 2. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on CAT phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 3. A computer copy is what the per-model guides call the most economical method — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 4. A microSD card is the local option the S53 datasheet names — expandable with microSD, which uses the second SIM slot. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, the S75's and the S53's card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM (the S62 Pro has a dedicated slot), and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The microSD card shares the SIM tray on the S75 and the S53. Both take a microSDXC card in the shared SIM slot, so a card and a second SIM compete for the same tray — but a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. The S62 Pro has a dedicated microSDXC slot, so no tray-sharing there — but a card is still not a USB drive. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current CAT — the S75, S62 Pro, and S53 all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. The per-model backup guides' most economical method backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a per-model FAQ for a phone-to-USB guide. The devicesfaq page for the S75 is a real CAT backup page — but its backup advice is a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos. It never describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking satellite messaging for a backup. The S75's Bullitt Satellite Messenger sends messages where there is no cellular coverage — that is messaging, not photos. Satellite messaging moves no files to a drive at all.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. It never describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone. The OKT3 and C32 pages say the same thing, word for word.; Mistaking OTG reverse charging for a backup. The WP33 Pro can act as a power bank and charge other devices over OTG — that is power going out of the phone, not photos. Reverse charging moves no files at all.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the WP39 and the WP35 both take a card up to 2 TB, and the WP33 Pro takes one up to 1 TB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. On the WP39 and the WP35 the card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Oukitel the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..
### Back up AGM photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/agm-photos-to-usb.html

AGM rugged phones (H6, H6 Pro, and H6 Lite) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB On-The-Go as Yes for the H6 and the H6 Pro, and USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go for the H6 Lite, and AGM's own product page lists OTG among the H6's features — and AGM has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the H6 manual's storage mention is Drive, Google's cloud, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current AGM. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On any USB-C AGM, plug a USB drive in: it mounts on plug-in on most models — the H6 and the H6 Pro list USB On-The-Go as Yes, and the H6 Lite lists USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the Google Photos community answer is to download the photos from Google Photos to the phone and then move them to USB with Files by Google, and Files by Google can access USB storage on Android 7.0 and later — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; AGM's own backup routes work too, but they are Google backup and Google Photos, which back your photos up to Google's cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. A manual, not a guide — and the confirmation that AGM's own storage route is the cloud, not a USB drive.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is an AGM-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated AGM photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: An AGM phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the H6 and the H6 Pro list USB On-The-Go as Yes, and the H6 Lite lists USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the current models, while a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three AGM specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current H6 family — spec tables list USB On-The-Go as Yes for the H6 and the H6 Pro, and USB Type-C with USB On-The-Go for the H6 Lite, and AGM's own product page lists OTG among the H6's features. Second, AGM has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the H6 manual's storage mention is Drive, Google's cloud, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos; AGM camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The H6 has a 3-card slot — two Nano SIM slots and a dedicated microSD slot, up to 512GB on AGM's own product page — so a card is an option, and unlike the hybrid slots on other rugged phones it does not cost you a second SIM, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: AGM's own tools (Google backup, Google Photos, Drive — not phone-to-USB). If you want AGM's own route, know what each tool actually does — the H6 manual's storage mention is Drive, Google's cloud, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google backup is the first way the stock guides describe — Settings > Google > All services > Backup, "Backup by Google One" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 2. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on AGM phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 3. A computer copy is the generic economical method — the H6 manual says the USB-C port is "for charging and data transfer", so connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 4. A microSD card is the local option AGM's own product page names — the H6 has a 3-card slot with two Nano SIM slots and a dedicated microSD slot, up to 512GB. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The microSD card is dedicated, not shared. The H6's 3-card slot gives the microSD card its own slot alongside two Nano SIMs, so a card never costs you a second SIM — but a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. Cloud storage moves no files to a USB drive at all.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The microSD card shares the SIM tray. The KingKong X takes a card up to 1 TB and the KingKong 11 takes one too, but on a shared SIM slot, so a card costs you a second SIM — and a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Cubot — the KingKong X, KingKong 11, KingKong Mini 4, and KingKong Dura all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. The generic backup guides' most economical method backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a per-model backup page for a phone-to-USB guide. The mobilespecs pages for the X11 and the KingKong Mini 3 are real Cubot backup pages — but their backup advice is Google cloud sync, Google Photos, or TWRP, CWM, and Titanium Backup. None of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking root-only tools for a normal backup. TWRP Recovery and Titanium Backup are real backup tools — but they need a custom recovery or root, which is a different job from backing up photos, and neither one copies your camera roll to a USB drive in one tap.; Mistaking the manual's Google backup for a USB backup. The P40 manual lists backup data to Google's servers — that is Google's cloud storage, not a copy to a drive you hold. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Cubot the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Unihertz photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/unihertz-photos-to-usb.html

Unihertz phones (Titan 2, Titan Pocket, Jelly 2, Jelly Star, and Tank) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB On-The-Go as Yes for the Tank, USB on-the-go for the Titan Pocket and the Tank 2, USB OTG for the Titan 2, and USB OTG for the Jelly 2 and the Jelly Star — and Unihertz has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model FAQ pages all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Unihertz. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On any USB-C Unihertz, plug a USB drive in: it mounts on plug-in on most models — the Tank lists USB On-The-Go as Yes, the Titan Pocket and the Tank 2 list USB on-the-go, the Titan 2 lists USB OTG, and the Jelly 2 and the Jelly Star list USB OTG — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — Pixoneye's route is to copy local originals to compatible USB storage with a file manager, and Files by Google can access USB storage on Android 7.0 and later — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Unihertz's own backup routes work too, but they are a computer copy, Google Drive, and Google Photos, which back your photos up to a PC or to Google's cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. If you want Hotwav's own route, know what each tool actually does — the user manuals for the Note 13 Max, the Note 13 Pro, and the Cyber 13 Pro all point to the same thing, "Regularly back up your data to cloud storage or an external device to prevent data loss", and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Hotwav phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup the manuals name — "back up your data to cloud storage" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A computer copy is the "external device" route in practice — connect the phone to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser — it backs your files up to a computer. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 4. A TF card is the local option the spec tables name — the Note 13 Max takes a TF card up to 1 TB, the Note 13 Pro takes one up to 1 TB, and the Cyber 13 Pro takes one up to 2 TB. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, the card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The TF card shares the SIM tray. The Note 13 Max takes a TF card up to 1 TB, the Note 13 Pro takes one up to 1 TB, and the Cyber 13 Pro takes one up to 2 TB, but on a shared SIM slot, so a card costs you a second SIM — and a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Hotwav — the Cyber 13 Pro, the Note 13 Pro, and the Note 13 Max all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive. The OTG cable is already in the box for all three models.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Coolmuster's Android Assistant and Dr.Fone's PC software back your phone up — but they are copies to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a user manual for a phone-to-USB guide. The manuals for the Note 13 Max, the Note 13 Pro, and the Cyber 13 Pro are real Hotwav backup pages — but their backup advice is to regularly back up your data to cloud storage or an external device. None of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking a TF card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a TF card is a real local copy — the Cyber 13 Pro takes a card up to 2 TB — but the card stays in the phone, it shares the SIM tray with the second SIM, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Hotwav the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up IIIF150 photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/iiif150-photos-to-usb.html

IIIF150 phones (B3C, Air3, and B2 Ultra) have USB-C and OTG across the range: the B3C spec table lists OTG as Support, the Air3 and the B2 Ultra list USB On-The-Go as Yes, and the Air1 Ultra and the Air2 Ultra list it too — and IIIF150 has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model FAQ pages point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current IIIF150. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:On any USB-C IIIF150, plug a USB drive in: it mounts on plug-in on most models — the B3C spec table lists OTG as Support, the B3C manual says to connect flash drives via an OTG adapter to the Type-C port, and the Air3, the B2 Ultra, the Air1 Ultra, the Air2 Ultra, and the Raptor all list USB On-The-Go as Yes — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — Dr.Fone's route is an OTG adapter copy, Google Drive, drag-and-drop through a PC, or AirDroid, and AnExplorer's route is an OTG file-manager copy — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; IIIF150's own backup advice works too, but it is a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, which back your photos up to a PC or to Google's cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a RugGear guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google Drive backs your data up to Google's cloud with 15 GB free, and Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a RugGear-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated RugGear photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A RugGear Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the RG655 runs Android 11, the RG850 runs Android 8.1 Oreo, and the RG880 runs Android 13 — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the RG850 and the RG880, while the RG655 has a micro USB port and needs a micro-USB OTG adapter for a regular USB drive — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three RugGear specifics: first, OTG is confirmed on the RG655 — the spec table lists USB OTG as Yes — and on the RG310 and the RG935 tablet, but the RG850 and RG880 datasheets I found do not list OTG either way, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it on those models. Second, RugGear has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the RG655 manual gives no backup advice at all; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; RugGear camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The RG655 takes a microSD card up to 128GB in FAT32 format, the RG850 takes one up to 128GB, and the RG880 takes one too, but on a hybrid SIM slot — so a card is an option, and it costs you a second SIM, and the card still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Note the RG655's own card reader does not support exFAT, so a microSD card over 4 GB per file is not an option on that phone either — another reason to use a USB drive.
Method 3: Method 3: RugGear's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want RugGear's own route, know what each tool actually does — the RG655 manual gives no backup advice at all, so there is no RugGear backup page to point at, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on RugGear Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option RugGear documents — the RG655 takes a card up to 128GB in FAT32 format, the RG850 takes one up to 128GB, and the RG880 takes one too. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, the card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM, the RG655's card reader does not support exFAT, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — connect the phone to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The RG170 and RG360 are not Android phones. RugGear's compact PTT handsets run a proprietary OS, not Android, so SnapDisk — which needs Android 7.0 or later — cannot install on them at all. This article is for the Android RugGear phones (RG655, RG850, RG880) and the RG935 tablet.; OTG is not confirmed on every RugGear model. The RG655 spec table lists USB OTG as Yes, the RG310 lists USB on-the-go, and the RG935 tablet lists OTG as supported — but the RG850 and RG880 datasheets I found do not list OTG either way, so confirm the drive mounts in Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the RG850 and the RG880, which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive. The RG655 has a micro USB port, so it needs a micro-USB OTG adapter, not a USB-C one. A plain micro-USB charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Dr.Fone's PC software backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a user manual for a phone-to-USB guide. The FindPare spec table for the RG655 and the RG655 user manual are real RugGear pages — but the spec table only lists OTG as Yes, and the manual gives no backup advice at all. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the RG655 takes a card up to 128GB — but the card stays in the phone, it shares the SIM tray with the second SIM, the RG655's card reader does not support exFAT, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On RugGear the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a PTT handset. The RG170 and the RG360 run a proprietary OS, not Android — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on them. If your RugGear has a 2.4-inch or 3-inch screen and a physical keypad with no Play Store, it is one of those handsets, not an Android phone.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

Sonim's Android phones (XP8 and XP10) have USB host support on at least the XP8 — the XP8 user guide lists the USB-C port as "High Speed, OTG" — and Sonim has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: Sonim SCOUT is a device-management app, not a backup, and the stock photo backup is Google Photos. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the YouTube guides' route is an OTG adapter copy with the built-in file manager, and askfilo's route is the same — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Kyocera's own backup advice works too, but there is none pointing at a USB drive — devicesfaq's advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser, or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud, which back your photos up to Google's servers, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A Kyocera DuraForce Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the Pro 2 runs Android 8.0, the Ultra 5G runs Android 10, the DuraSport runs Android 11, and the PRO 3 runs Android 13 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Kyocera specifics: first, OTG is confirmed on the Pro 2 — the spec tables list USB OTG as Yes — and on the DuraSport — its spec pages list the port as "USB Type-C, USB On-The-Go" — but the Ultra 5G and PRO 3 datasheets I found do not list OTG either way, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it on those models. Second, Kyocera has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; Kyocera camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The Pro 2 takes a microSD card up to 512GB, the Ultra 5G and the DuraSport take one up to 1TB, and the PRO 3 takes one up to 2TB — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: Method 3: Kyocera's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Kyocera's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Kyocera backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Kyocera Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option Kyocera documents — the Pro 2 takes a card up to 512GB, the Ultra 5G and the DuraSport take one up to 1TB, and the PRO 3 takes one up to 2TB — and Verizon's own support page walks through moving files from internal storage to the card. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — connect the phone to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The older DuraForce phones are out of scope. The original DuraForce runs Android 4.4.2 and the DuraForce XD runs Android 5.1, so SnapDisk — which needs Android 7.0 or later — cannot install on them at all; the original DuraForce PRO's spec tables list USB OTG as No, so it cannot host a USB drive either. The DuraXV flip phones are a different shape of phone — keypad flips with a small screen — and this article is for the DuraForce smartphones (Pro 2, Ultra 5G, PRO 3, and DuraSport).; OTG is not confirmed on every Kyocera model. The spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the Pro 2, and the DuraSport's spec pages list its port as "USB Type-C, USB On-The-Go" — but the Ultra 5G and PRO 3 datasheets I found do not list OTG either way, so confirm the drive mounts in Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into all four DuraForce phones, which all have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Kyocera's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a user manual for a phone-to-USB guide. The Pro 2 GSMArena page and the PRO 3 spec sheet are real Kyocera pages — but the spec table only lists the port as USB Type-C 3.1, and the spec sheet only lists "Superspeed USB 3.2 Gen 1, Type-C". Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the Pro 2 takes a card up to 512GB, the Ultra 5G and the DuraSport up to 1TB, and the PRO 3 up to 2TB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Kyocera the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Kyocera that is too old to run it. The original DuraForce runs Android 4.4.2 and the DuraForce XD runs Android 5.1 — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on them — and the original DuraForce PRO has no USB OTG at all. If your Kyocera has a micro-USB port and a 2016 release date, it is one of those handsets, not a current DuraForce.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Crosscall photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Crosscall's rugged Android phones (Core-X5, Action-X5, Core-Z5, and Stellar-X5) have USB host support on at least three of them — the spec tables list USB On-The-Go support as Yes for the Core-X5, Crosscall's own product sheet lists OTG as Yes for the Action-X5, and the Core-Z5 spec tables list USB On-The-Go support as Yes — and Crosscall has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. One honest caveat up front: the Stellar-X5 spec pages I found list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it on that model, and the older Trekker-M1 phones are out of scope — they run Android 5.1, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

None of them is a Crosscall-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Crosscall photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A Crosscall rugged Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the Core-X5 runs Android 11, the Action-X5 runs Android 11, the Core-Z5 runs Android 12, and the Stellar-X5 runs Android 13 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Crosscall specifics: first, OTG is confirmed on the Core-X5 — the spec tables list USB On-The-Go support as Yes — on the Action-X5 — Crosscall's own product sheet lists OTG as Yes — and on the Core-Z5 — the spec tables list USB On-The-Go support as Yes — but the Stellar-X5 spec pages I found do not list OTG either way, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it on that model. Second, Crosscall has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; Crosscall camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The Core-X5 takes a microSD card up to 512GB, the Action-X5 takes one up to 512GB, and the Core-Z5 takes one up to 1TB — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: Method 3: Crosscall's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Crosscall's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Crosscall backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Crosscall Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option Crosscall documents — the Core-X5 takes a card up to 512GB, the Action-X5 takes one up to 512GB, and the Core-Z5 takes one up to 1TB — and the Trekker-X4 manual walks through moving files to a computer instead. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — "Using a USB cable, connect your device to a computer" and transfer the files between your device and your computer, per the Trekker-X4 manual. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The older Trekker-M1 phones are out of scope. The Trekker-M1 and the Trekker-M1 Core run Android 5.1, so SnapDisk — which needs Android 7.0 or later — cannot install on them at all. If your Crosscall has a micro-USB port and a 2016 release date, it is one of those handsets, not a current rugged phone.; OTG is not confirmed on every Crosscall model. The spec tables list USB On-The-Go support as Yes for the Core-X5, Crosscall's own product sheet lists OTG as Yes for the Action-X5, and the Core-Z5 spec tables list USB On-The-Go support as Yes — but the Stellar-X5 spec pages I found do not list OTG either way, so confirm the drive mounts in Settings > Storage on that model before relying on it. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later.
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into all four Crosscall phones, which all have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Crosscall's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a user manual for a phone-to-USB guide. The Core-X5 manuals.ca page and the Stellar-X5 spec table are real Crosscall pages — but the spec table only lists the port as USB Type-C, and the manual only lists "USB On-The-Go support: Yes". Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the Core-X5 takes a card up to 512GB, the Action-X5 up to 512GB, and the Core-Z5 up to 1TB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Crosscall the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Crosscall that is too old to run it. The Trekker-M1 and the Trekker-M1 Core run Android 5.1 — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on them. If your Crosscall has a micro-USB port and a 2016 release date, it is one of those handsets, not a current rugged phone.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this.

### Back up Hammer photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/hammer-photos-to-usb.html

Hammer's rugged Android phones (Blade V 5G, Iron 4, Blade 3, and Explorer Pro) have USB-C ports, and the only per-model OTG listings I found are FindPare's — USB OTG as Yes for the Energy 18x9 and the Blade 2 Pro — but FindPare itself says its information is not ascertained, and the current models' spec pages list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it — and Hammer has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. One honest caveat up front: the Hammer 6 LTE is a feature phone, not an Android phone at all, so SnapDisk cannot install on it, and the original Hammer Iron runs Android 4.2 and the AXE M LTE runs Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:On a Hammer rugged Android phone with USB host support, plug a USB drive in — the only per-model OTG listings I found are FindPare's, USB OTG as Yes for the Energy 18x9 and the Blade 2 Pro, but FindPare itself says its information is not ascertained, so treat those as leads and test with a drive, and the current Blade V 5G, Iron 4, Blade 3, and Explorer Pro spec pages list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the YouTube guides' route is an OTG adapter copy with the built-in file manager, and askfilo's route is the same — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Hammer's own backup advice works too, but there is none pointing at a USB drive — devicesfaq's advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser, or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud, which back your photos up to Google's servers, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the Blade V 5G takes a card up to 1TB, and the Blade 3, the Iron 4, and the Explorer Pro take one up to 128GB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Hammer the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Hammer that is too old to run it — or is not an Android phone at all. The Hammer 6 LTE is a feature phone, not an Android phone, and the original Hammer Iron runs Android 4.2 and the AXE M LTE runs Android 6.0 — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on any of them. If your Hammer has a keypad and an SOS button, or a micro-USB port and a 2016–2017 release date, it is one of those handsets, not a current rugged Android phone.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

What you need: A FOSSiBOT F-series Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the F101 Pro and the F101P run Android 13, the F102 runs Android 13, and the F107 Pro and the F113 run Android 15 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three FOSSiBOT specifics: first, OTG is confirmed on most of the line — the spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the F101, the F101 PRO, the F102, the F110 Pro 5G, and the F113, the F112 Pro's spec page lists USB OTG Type-C, and the F107 Pro's official-site spec says you can connect USB flash drives via an OTG cable — but the F101P's official page mentions OTG only as reverse charging and the F115 Ultra's spec data conflicts, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it on those two models. Second, FOSSiBOT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; the stock file manager is Files by Google; FOSSiBOT camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The F101 Pro takes a microSD card up to 1 TB, and the F107 Pro and the F113 take one up to 2 TB — the F102's card size is the one disagreement in my sources, 1 TB per RottenWifi and 2 TB per Cashify — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Method 3: FOSSiBOT's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want FOSSiBOT's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no FOSSiBOT backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on FOSSiBOT Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option FOSSiBOT documents — the F101 Pro takes a card up to 1 TB, and the F107 Pro and the F113 take one up to 2 TB, with the F102's card size disputed between sources (1 TB per RottenWifi, 2 TB per Cashify) — and the F107 Pro's own spec page names the card slot alongside the OTG cable. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — "connect the FOSSiBOT F102 to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser", per devicesfaq. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; OTG is not confirmed on every FOSSiBOT model. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later.; The oldest FOSSiBOT phone is out of scope until checked. Every other F-series model I found runs Android 13 or 15..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the F101, the F101 Pro, the F102, the F107 Pro, the F110 Pro 5G, the F112 Pro, and the F113, which all have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. FOSSiBOT's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a user manual for a phone-to-USB guide. The F107 Pro manual page and the F102 FAQ page are real FOSSiBOT pages — but the manual only mentions OTG as reverse charging ("10W OTG reverse charging, allowing you to power other devices"), and the FAQ only says to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files with a file browser. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking "OTG reverse charging" for OTG host support. The F101P's official page and the F107 Pro manual both mention OTG reverse charging — that is the phone sharing its battery with another device, not the phone reading a flash drive. The host evidence for the F107 Pro is the official-site spec saying flash drives connect via an OTG cable; for the F101P there is no host evidence at all, so test with a drive.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. That means that you can connect flash drives or an external HDD to this mobile phone", with USB-C and a hybrid slot. A retailer spec page, not a guide — and the confirmation that the Bison Plus lists OTG.; Umidigi Bison 2 Pro, MySmartPrice (Umidigi Bison 2 Pro) — Android 12, "USB Type-C, Mass storage device, USB charging, USB On-The-Go" and "USB OTG Support, Yes", with 256 GB of storage and a microSD slot up to 512 GB. A spec comparison, not a guide — and the confirmation that the Bison X10 and X10G list OTG.; Umidigi Bison X10G vs Bison X10 Pro, phonesdata (Bison X10G vs Bison X10 Pro) — "USB: USB Type-C, OTG" for the X10G and "Yes, USB Type C, USB On-The-Go (OTG)" for the X10 Pro.
