A review, not a guide — and the confirmation that the X20's OTG mention is reverse charging only, which powers another device and is not hosting a drive.; Umidigi Bison GT2 Pro 5G, gsmfind (Umidigi Bison GT2 Pro 5G) — Android 12, "USB: USB Type-C", with no OTG mention; the GT2 Pro page (Umidigi Bison GT2 Pro) lists the same, Android 12 with "USB: USB Type-C". Spec tables, not guides — and the confirmation that neither GT2 Pro model lists OTG in the sources I found.; Frequently asked questions UMIDIGI BISON GT2 PRO 5G, devicesfaq (BISON GT2 PRO 5G FAQ) — "Check the BISON GT2 PRO 5G's 2.0 OTG Type-C charging port, for example, with a flashlight" and "it comes from the factory with the Android 11 operating system", against gsmfind's Android 12. A FAQ page, not a backup guide — and the confirmation that the GT2 Pro 5G's OTG mention is about the charging port, and its Android version is disputed between sources.; Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Google Play) — the one-tap app alternative: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit. It is free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a UMIDIGI Bison guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google Drive backs your data up to Google's cloud with 15 GB free, and Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a UMIDIGI Bison-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated UMIDIGI Bison photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A UMIDIGI Bison Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the Bison runs Android 10, the Bison Pro and the Bison Plus run Android 11, and the Bison 2 Pro runs Android 12 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three UMIDIGI specifics: first, OTG is confirmed on most of the line — the spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the Bison, the Bison Pro, the Bison Plus, the Bison 2 Pro, the Bison X10, the Bison X10G, and the Bison X10 Pro — but the Bison X20's OTG host support is unverified and the Bison GT, the Bison GT2 Pro, the Bison GT2 Pro 5G, the Bison X10S, and the Bison X10S NFC have no OTG listing in the sources I found, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it on those models. Second, UMIDIGI has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; the stock file manager is Files by Google; UMIDIGI camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The Bison Pro takes a microSD card up to 256 GB, the Bison 2 Pro takes one up to 512 GB, and the Bison X20 takes one up to 1 TB — the original Bison's card size is the one disagreement in my sources, 256 GB per MySmartPrice and 128 GB per mobility.com.ng — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Method 3: UMIDIGI's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want UMIDIGI's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no UMIDIGI backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on UMIDIGI Bison Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option UMIDIGI documents — the Bison Pro takes a card up to 256 GB, the Bison 2 Pro takes one up to 512 GB, and the Bison X20 takes one up to 1 TB, with the original Bison's card size disputed between sources (256 GB per MySmartPrice, 128 GB per mobility.com.ng) — and the Bison FAQ names passing media files to a memory card as one of the backup steps. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — "connect the UMIDIGI BISON to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser", per devicesfaq, and the same advice appears on the Bison GT, Bison Pro, Bison X10, Bison X10 Pro, Bison X10S, X10S NFC, Bison 2021, and GT2 5G pages. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; OTG is not confirmed on every Bison model. The spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the Bison, the Bison Pro, the Bison Plus, the Bison 2 Pro, the Bison X10, the Bison X10G, and the Bison X10 Pro — but the Bison X20's OTG host support is unverified (one source lists OTG Support as No, the others list USB Type-C only, and the reviews mention OTG reverse charging only, which powers another device and is not hosting a drive), and the Bison GT, the Bison GT2 Pro, the Bison GT2 Pro 5G, the Bison X10S, and the Bison X10S NFC have no OTG listing in the sources I found, so confirm the drive mounts in Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later.; The original Bison's connector is disputed. GSMArena and MySmartPrice list the original Bison as USB-C, while mobility.com.ng lists it as microUSB v2.0 — so check your own port before buying an adapter: a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a USB-C port, while a micro-USB port needs a micro-USB OTG adapter instead.; The Bison X10 models' Android versions are unverified. I did not verify the Android version of the Bison X10, the Bison X10G, or the Bison X10 Pro in the sources above, so owners of those models should check Settings > About phone first — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on anything older. Every other Bison model I found runs Android 10, 11, 12, or 13..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the Bison, the Bison Pro, the Bison Plus, the Bison 2 Pro, the Bison X10, the Bison X10G, and the Bison X10 Pro, which all have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction. And if your original Bison turns out to have the microUSB port that mobility.com.ng lists instead of the USB-C that GSMArena and MySmartPrice list, you need a micro-USB OTG adapter, not a USB-C one — check the port first.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. UMIDIGI's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a FAQ page for a phone-to-USB guide. The Bison FAQ page and the Bison spec tables are real UMIDIGI pages — but the FAQ only says to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files with a file browser, and the spec tables only list "USB OTG: Yes". Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking "OTG reverse charging" for OTG host support. The Bison X20 reviews mention OTG reverse charging — that is the phone sharing its battery with another device, not the phone reading a flash drive. The host evidence for the X20 is absent: one source lists OTG Support as No and the others list USB Type-C only, so test with a drive.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the Bison Pro takes a card up to 256 GB, the Bison 2 Pro takes one up to 512 GB, and the Bison X20 takes one up to 1 TB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On UMIDIGI the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Bison that is too old to run it. The Bison X10, X10G, and X10 Pro have unverified Android versions in my sources — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later. Check Settings > About phone before installing on those models; every other Bison model I found runs Android 10, 11, 12, or 13.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Energizer photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/energizer-photos-to-usb.html

Energizer's rugged Hard Case line is made by Avenir Telecom under an exclusive Energizer brand license, and Energizer has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. Four honest caveats up front: no Hard Case model lists USB OTG support in the sources I found — the spec tables list USB Type-C for the H550S, the H570S, the H590S, and the H620S and microUSB 2.0 for the H500S, with no OTG mention on any of them — so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it; the H280S and the H242S run KaiOS, not Android, so SnapDisk cannot run on them at all; the H240S runs Android 6.0 with no Google Play access, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum; and the H570S specs are disputed between sources — Android 8.0 with a Helio P18, 3 GB of RAM, 32 GB of storage, and a 4800 mAh battery per Gadgets360's 2018 launch story, against Android 9.0 with a MediaTek MT6739, 2 GB of RAM, 16 GB of storage, and a 6500 mAh battery per phonesdata, specspro, and others — so check Settings > About phone on that model. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:On an Energizer Hard Case Android phone that mounts a USB drive, plug the drive in — no Hard Case model lists USB OTG support in the sources I found, so test with a drive and confirm it appears in Settings > Storage first — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the YouTube guides' route is an OTG connection with the built-in file manager, and askfilo's route is the same — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Energizer's own backup advice works too, but there is none pointing at a USB drive — devicesfaq's advice for the H550S is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser, or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud, which back your photos up to Google's servers, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. It is a generic Android listing, not an Energizer guide, and it needs a USB-C connection — so it is no use on the microUSB Hard Case models.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google Drive backs your data up to Google's cloud with 15 GB free, and Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is an Energizer-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Energizer photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: An Energizer Hard Case Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the H550S runs Android 7.0, exactly the minimum, the H590S runs Android 8.0, the H620S runs Android 10, and the H621S runs Android 11 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the H550S, the H570S, the H590S, and the H620S, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter, and the H500S and the Energy E500S have microUSB 2.0 instead, so they need a micro-USB OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Four Energizer specifics: first, OTG is unconfirmed across the whole Hard Case line — no Hard Case model lists USB OTG support in the sources I found, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it on any model; the only Energizer OTG listing I found is the cancelled Ultimate U620S Pop, which is a different line and was never sold. Second, not every Hard Case phone can run SnapDisk at all — the H280S and the H242S run KaiOS, not Android, and the H240S runs Android 6.0 with no Google Play access, so all three are out; the H500S Android version is disputed between sources (Android 8.0 per pkgsm, Android 7.0 per mobilespecs and spec411), and the H570S specs are disputed wholesale, so owners of those two models should check Settings > About phone first. Third, Energizer has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; the stock file manager is Files by Google; Energizer camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The H550S takes a microSD card up to 32 GB, the H500S takes one up to 64 GB, and the H240S takes one up to 32 GB — the H570S card size is the one disagreement in my sources, up to 32 GB per phonesdata and up to 128 GB per Gadgets360 — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Fourth, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Method 3: Energizer's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Energizer's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Energizer backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Energizer Hard Case Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option Energizer documents — the H550S takes a card up to 32 GB, the H500S takes one up to 64 GB, and the H240S takes one up to 32 GB, with the H570S card size disputed between sources (up to 32 GB per phonesdata, up to 128 GB per Gadgets360). It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — "connect the Energizer Hardcase H550S to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser", per devicesfaq, and the same advice appears on the H590S, H620S, H501S, H240S, H280S, and H242 pages. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; OTG is not confirmed on any Hard Case model. No Hard Case model lists USB OTG support in the sources I found — the spec tables list USB Type-C for the H550S, the H570S, the H590S, and the H620S and microUSB 2.0 for the H500S, with no OTG mention on any of them — so confirm the drive mounts in Settings > Storage before relying on it. The only Energizer OTG listing I found is the cancelled Ultimate U620S Pop, a different line that was never sold, so it says nothing about the Hard Case phones. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later.; Two Hard Case models cannot run SnapDisk at all. The H280S and the H242S run KaiOS, not Android — there is no Android app to install on them, and their photos move off the phone by computer copy or microSD card instead. The H240S runs Android 6.0 with no Google Play access, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so it is out too.; The H570S specs are disputed. Gadgets360's 2018 launch story lists Android 8.0, a Helio P18, 3 GB of RAM, 32 GB of storage, microSD up to 128 GB, and a 4800 mAh battery, while phonesdata, specspro, and others list Android 9.0, a MediaTek MT6739, 2 GB of RAM, 16 GB of storage, microSD up to 32 GB, and a 6500 mAh battery, announced February 2019 — so check Settings > About phone on that model before trusting either spec set. Either way it runs Android 7.0 or later, so SnapDisk installs if the phone mounts a drive.; The H500S Android version is disputed. pkgsm lists Android 8.0, while mobilespecs and spec411 list Android 7.0 — so check Settings > About phone first. Either way it runs Android 7.0 or later, so SnapDisk installs if the phone mounts a drive; its port is microUSB 2.0 in every source, so it needs a micro-USB OTG adapter, not a USB-C one.; The H621S connector is unverified. I found the H621S runs Android 11 with 64 GB of storage, but no USB or OTG detail in the page I found — so check your own port before buying an adapter. SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later, which the H621S clears..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the H550S, the H570S, the H590S, and the H620S, which all have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. The H500S and the Energy E500S have microUSB 2.0 instead, so they need a micro-USB OTG adapter. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction. And the H621S connector is unverified in my sources — check the port first.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Energizer's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a FAQ page for a phone-to-USB guide. The H550S FAQ page and the Hard Case spec tables are real Energizer pages — but the FAQ only says to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files with a file browser, and the spec tables only list a USB connector type with no OTG mention. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking the Ultimate U620S Pop's OTG listing for a Hard Case listing. GSMArena lists "USB Type-C 2.0, OTG" for the Ultimate U620S Pop — but that phone was cancelled, it is from the Ultimate line, not the Hard Case line, and it was never sold. It says nothing about whether a Hard Case phone hosts a drive. Test with a drive.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the H550S takes a card up to 32 GB, the H500S takes one up to 64 GB, and the H240S takes one up to 32 GB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Energizer the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Hard Case phone that cannot run it. The H280S and the H242S run KaiOS, not Android, and the H240S runs Android 6.0 with no Google Play access — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on any of the three. Check Settings > About phone before installing; every other Hard Case model I found runs Android 7.0, 8.0, 9.0, 10, or 11.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Nomu photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/nomu-photos-to-usb.html

Nomu's rugged line lists USB OTG support on most models, and Nomu has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. Four honest caveats up front: three models run Android 6.0 — the S10, the S20, and the S30 — below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so SnapDisk cannot run on them at all, even though the S20 and the S30 list OTG support; the S10's OTG support is unconfirmed — PhoneMore lists microUSB 2.0 with no OTG mention — so check Settings > Storage on that model before relying on it; the specs are disputed between sources on several models — the S20 chipset (MediaTek MT6735 per Review Hub, MT6737T per UL benchmarks), the T18 chipset (MT6737 per gizmochina, MT6737T per unite4buy), the M8 Android version (7.0 per phonesdata and devicesfaq, 7.1 per unite4buy) and battery (2950 mAh per devicesfaq, 3000 mAh per unite4buy), and the microSD size on the S10 Pro (up to 64 GB per PhoneMore, up to 32 GB per Smartprix), the S30 (up to 64 GB per PhoneMore, up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck), and the M6 (up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck, up to 64 GB per unite4buy) — so check Settings > About phone on those models; and the M8 is the only Nomu model I found with a USB-C port — every other model has microUSB 2.0 — so the rest need a micro-USB OTG adapter, not a USB-C one. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:On a Nomu phone that runs Android 7.0 and mounts a USB drive — the S10 Pro, the S30 Mini, the M6, the M8, and the T18 — plug the drive in, then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the YouTube guides' route is an OTG connection with the built-in file manager, and askfilo's route is the same — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Nomu's own backup advice works too, but there is none pointing at a USB drive — devicesfaq's advice for the S10 is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser, or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud, which back your photos up to Google's servers, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option Nomu documents — the S10 takes a card up to 64 GB, the S30 Mini takes one up to 64 GB, and the T18 takes one up to 32 GB, with the S10 Pro, S30, and M6 card sizes disputed between sources (up to 64 GB per PhoneMore against up to 32 GB per Smartprix on the S10 Pro; up to 64 GB per PhoneMore against up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck on the S30; up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck against up to 64 GB per unite4buy on the M6). It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — "connect the Nomu S10 to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser", per devicesfaq, and the same advice appears on the S30 Mini page. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; Three Nomu models cannot run SnapDisk at all. The S10, the S20, and the S30 run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum — so SnapDisk cannot install on any of the three, even though the S20 and the S30 list OTG support. Their photos move off the phone by file manager or computer copy instead.; The S10's OTG support is unconfirmed. PhoneMore lists the S10 as microUSB 2.0 with no OTG mention, and no OTG in its feature list — so confirm the drive mounts in Settings > Storage before relying on it. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later, which the S10 does not have.; The specs are disputed on several models. The S20 chipset is MediaTek MT6735 per Review Hub against MT6737T per UL benchmarks; the T18 chipset is MT6737 per gizmochina against MT6737T per unite4buy; the M8 Android version is 7.0 per phonesdata and devicesfaq against 7.1 per unite4buy, and its battery is 2950 mAh per devicesfaq against 3000 mAh per unite4buy; the microSD size is disputed on the S10 Pro (up to 64 GB per PhoneMore, up to 32 GB per Smartprix), the S30 (up to 64 GB per PhoneMore, up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck), and the M6 (up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck, up to 64 GB per unite4buy) — so check Settings > About phone on those models before trusting either spec set. Either way the S10 Pro, the S30 Mini, the M6, the M8, and the T18 run Android 7.0, so SnapDisk installs if the phone mounts a drive.; The M8 is the only Nomu model with USB-C. phonesdata lists the M8 as USB Type-C with OTG, and devicesfaq lists USB Type-C with no OTG mention — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the M8, while the S10 Pro, the S30 Mini, the M6, and the T18 have microUSB 2.0 and need a micro-USB OTG adapter. Check your own port before buying an adapter..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A micro-USB OTG adapter is what the S10 Pro, the S30 Mini, the M6, and the T18 need for a regular USB-A drive, since all four have microUSB 2.0 — so a USB-C OTG adapter is the wrong one for them. The M8 has USB-C instead, so it needs a USB-C OTG adapter for a regular USB-A drive, or a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. A plain micro-USB charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Nomu's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a FAQ page for a phone-to-USB guide. The S10 FAQ page and the Nomu spec tables are real Nomu pages — but the FAQ only says to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files with a file browser, and the spec tables only list "USB OTG" or a USB connector type. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG support for SnapDisk support. The S20 and the S30 both list OTG support — Review Hub lists "USB OTG: YES" for the S20, and PhoneMore and Notebookcheck list OTG for the S30 — but both run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. OTG lets a file manager copy photos to a drive; it does not make the phone new enough to install SnapDisk. Test with a drive, and use Method 2 or 4 on those models.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the S10 takes a card up to 64 GB, the S30 Mini takes one up to 64 GB, and the T18 takes one up to 32 GB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Nomu the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Nomu phone that cannot run it. The S10, the S20, and the S30 run Android 6.0 — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on any of the three. Check Settings > About phone before installing; every other Nomu model I found runs Android 7.0.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Conquest photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/conquest-photos-to-usb.html

Conquest makes rugged phones with big batteries and walkie-talkie hardware, and Conquest has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. Four honest caveats up front: four models cannot run SnapDisk at all — the S6 runs Android 5.1, and the S8, the S8+, and the S8 Pro run Android 6.0 — below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so SnapDisk cannot run on them at all, even though the S8 lists USB OTG support; the S9 is disputed between sources — Android 5.1.1 with a Snapdragon 615 per devicesfaq, Android 7.1.1 with a Helio P25 per trak.in — so check Settings > About phone on that model before installing; OTG support is confirmed in the sources I found only on the S8, which cannot run SnapDisk — on the S10, the S12, the S12 Pro, the S16, the S22 5G, and the EX201 it is unconfirmed, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it; and the USB port type is unconfirmed on the S22 5G and the EX201 — the S10 has micro USB, the S12 and the S16 have USB-C, and the S8 has micro USB 2.0 — so check your own port before buying an adapter. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On a Conquest phone that runs Android 7.0 and mounts a USB drive — the S10, the S12, the S12 Pro, the S16, the S22 5G, and the EX201 — plug the drive in, then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the YouTube guides' route is an OTG connection with the built-in file manager, and askfilo's route is the same — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Conquest's own backup advice works too, but there is none pointing at a USB drive — devicesfaq's advice for the S8 is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser, or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud, which back your photos up to Google's servers, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 18, 2026, no top search result for this query is a Conquest-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, let alone a Conquest-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the Conquest-specific results are FAQ pages that give no USB-drive advice at all, and the rest are generic manual guides.

Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a Conquest-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Conquest photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A Conquest Android phone that runs Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk — the S10 runs Android 7.1, the S12 runs Android 8.1, the S12 Pro runs Android 8.1, the S16 runs Android 9.0, the S22 5G runs Android 11, and the EX201 runs Android 12 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the S12 and the S16, which have USB-C, while the S10 has micro USB, so a regular USB-A drive needs a micro-USB OTG adapter on that model — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Four Conquest specifics: first, four models cannot run SnapDisk at all — the S6 runs Android 5.1, and the S8, the S8+, and the S8 Pro run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, even though the S8 lists USB OTG support, so their photos move off the phone by file manager or computer copy instead; the S9's Android version is disputed — 5.1.1 per devicesfaq, 7.1.1 per trak.in — so check Settings > About phone on that model before installing, since SnapDisk cannot run on it if the 5.1.1 source is right. Second, OTG support is confirmed in the sources I found only on the S8, which cannot run SnapDisk — on the S10, the S12, the S12 Pro, the S16, the S22 5G, and the EX201 it is unconfirmed, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it: if the drive appears, the phone hosts drives and the rest of this method works; if it never appears, the phone does not host drives and Method 4 is the route. Third, Conquest has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; the stock file manager is Files by Google; Conquest camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The S8+ takes a microSD card up to 128 GB, the S10 takes one up to 128 GB, and the S16 takes one up to 128 GB — the S16 ATEX variant takes one up to 2 TB — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Fourth, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Conquest Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. The S6 runs Android 5.1, and the S8, the S8+, and the S8 Pro run Android 6.0 — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on any of the four. Check Settings > About phone before installing; every other Conquest model I found runs Android 7.1, 8.1, 9.0, 11, or 12, except the S9, whose Android version is disputed.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A Land Rover Explore phone — either model runs Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk: the Explore runs Android 7.1 and the Explore R runs Android 9 with an upgrade to Android 10 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into either model, both of which have USB-C, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Two Land Rover specifics: first, OTG support is confirmed in the sources I found only on the original Explore — FindPare lists "USB OTG: Yes" and Notebookcheck's review says the USB-C connection "supports USB OTG" — while on the Explore R no source I found mentions OTG at all, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it: if the drive appears, the phone hosts drives and the rest of this method works; if it never appears, the phone does not host drives and Method 4 is the route. Second, Land Rover has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its manual's backup is Google backup to Google's servers; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; the stock file manager is Files by Google; Land Rover Explore camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone, and the camera shoots in RAW and records video at 4K, so the files are worth keeping as originals. Both models take a microSD card — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. The microSD capacity is unlisted in the sources I found, so check your own card before relying on it. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Method 3: Land Rover's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Land Rover's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Land Rover backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Land Rover Explore Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. Google backup is what the Explore manual itself names: personal settings back up to Google's servers with a Google account, and are restored to a new phone when you sign in with that account. It is a real backup — but it backs up settings, not a folder of photo files on a drive you hold. 4. A microSD card is the local option Land Rover documents — both the Explore and the Explore R take a microSD card. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 5. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — the manual moves music from a PC onto the phone with the USB power cable, and its FAQ moves files to a computer the same way, by connecting the phone with a USB cable and dragging files. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; OTG support is unconfirmed on the Explore R. The original Explore lists USB OTG support — FindPare lists "USB OTG: Yes" and Notebookcheck's review says the USB-C connection "supports USB OTG" — but no source I found mentions OTG on the Explore R at all, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on that model before relying on it. The drive mounting is the test.; One spec page disagrees about the Explore R. mobilespecs.net lists the Explore R as Android 7.0 with a MediaTek Helio X27 — the original Explore's spec — while mobiles4sale, UL benchmarks, and outdoorsmagic list it as Android 9 with a Helio P35, so that page is not used as a source for the Explore R here. Either way the Explore R clears SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum.; The microSD capacity is unlisted in the sources found. Both models take a microSD card, but no source I found states the maximum size, so check your own card before relying on it — and a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader.; Both models have USB-C, so the adapter is the same either way. The Explore and the Explore R both have a USB Type-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into either one and a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter on either one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into either Explore model, both of which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Land Rover's own file advice is a computer copy with a USB cable — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a manual page for a phone-to-USB guide. The Explore manual and the Land Rover Explore spec tables are real Land Rover pages — but the manual only says to back settings up to Google's servers and to move files with a USB cable to a computer, and the spec tables only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. The original Explore lists USB OTG support — FindPare lists "USB OTG: Yes" and Notebookcheck's review says the USB-C connection "supports USB OTG" — but no source I found mentions OTG on the Explore R. Test with a drive on the Explore R, and use Method 2 or 4 on that model if the drive never mounts.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — both Explore models take a microSD card — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. A retailer page, not a guide — and the confirmation that the E50 runs Android 16, with no OTG mention.; JCB Toughphone T10 Rugged Tablet, jcbphone.com (JCB Toughphone T10 Rugged Tablet) — JCB's own page: Android 16, 128 GB of storage expandable to 2 TB via microSD, and "18W wired, USB-C with OTG support". A product page, not a guide — and the confirmation, from JCB itself, that the T10 tablet lists OTG support and runs Android 16.; JCB Toughphone Pro-Smart Review, SlashGear (JCB Toughphone Pro-Smart Review) — the 2012 Toughphone Pro-Smart TP909 runs Android 2.3.5 Gingerbread on an 800 MHz single-core processor with 256 MB of ROM. A review, not a guide — and the confirmation that the old Pro-Smart runs Android 2.3.5, far below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so it cannot run SnapDisk at all.; Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Google Play) — the one-tap app alternative: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit. It is free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a JCB guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file.; PhotoSaver Phone-to-Drive (Google Play) — a second one-tap app alternative: save photos and videos to any USB-C drive with one click, no cloud, no upload. It is a generic Android listing, not a JCB guide — but it does work on the current JCB models, since all of them have USB-C.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google Drive backs your data up to Google's cloud with 15 GB free, and Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a JCB-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated JCB photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A JCB Toughphone — every current model runs Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk: the Toughphone runs Android 13, the Toughphone Max runs Android 12, the E10 runs Android 15, the E50 runs Android 16, and the T10 tablet runs Android 16 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current model, all of which have USB-C, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Two JCB specifics: first, OTG support is confirmed in the sources I found on the Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, the E10, and the T10 — cashify lists "OTG Support, Yes" for the Toughphone and the Toughphone Max, the E10 review lists "USB-C 2.0 (OTG)", and JCB's own T10 page lists "USB-C with OTG support" — while on the E50 no source I found mentions OTG at all, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it: if the drive appears, the phone hosts drives and the rest of this method works; if it never appears, the phone does not host drives and Method 4 is the route. Second, JCB has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the only JCB file advice found is the old TP802 manual's PC copy with a USB cable; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; the stock file manager is Files by Google; JCB Toughphone camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. All current models take a microSD card — up to 1 TB on the Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, and the E50, up to 512 GB on the E10, and up to 2 TB on the T10 tablet — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Method 3: JCB's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want JCB's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no JCB backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on JCB Toughphone Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. Google backup is what Android itself names: personal settings back up to Google's servers with a Google account, and are restored to a new phone when you sign in with that account. It is a real backup — but it backs up settings, not a folder of photo files on a drive you hold. 4. A microSD card is the local option on every current JCB model — the Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, and the E50 take a card up to 1 TB, the E10 up to 512 GB, and the T10 tablet up to 2 TB. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 5. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — the TP802 manual moves files to a computer by connecting the phone with a USB cable and selecting "Mass Storage". It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; OTG support is unconfirmed on the E50. The Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, the E10, and the T10 all list OTG support — cashify lists "OTG Support, Yes" for the Toughphone and the Toughphone Max, the E10 review lists "USB-C 2.0 (OTG)", and JCB's own T10 page lists "USB-C with OTG support" — but no source I found mentions OTG on the E50 at all, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on that model before relying on it. The drive mounting is the test.; The E10's specs are disputed between sources. One review's own spec table says Android 16 while its text and JCB's own site say Android 15; the same review says the chipset is a Helio G36, while Clove and rugged.co.uk say MT6765X; and the review says 4 GB of RAM while rugged.co.uk says 8 GB. The Android version is taken as 15 from JCB's own site, and the chipset and RAM are not leaned on here. Either way the E10 clears SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum.; Two old JCB phones cannot run SnapDisk at all. The TP802 is a feature phone, not an Android phone, and the Toughphone Pro-Smart TP909 from 2012 runs Android 2.3.5 Gingerbread — both are below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. On those phones the computer copy in Method 4 is the route.; All current models have USB-C, so the adapter is the same either way. The Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, the E10, the E50, and the T10 tablet all have a USB Type-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them and a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter on any of them. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current JCB model, all of which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. JCB's own file advice is a computer copy with a USB cable — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a manual page for a phone-to-USB guide. The TP802 manual and the JCB Toughphone spec pages are real JCB pages — but the manual only says to connect to a PC with a USB cable and copy files as Mass Storage, and the spec pages only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. The Toughphone, the Toughphone Max, the E10, and the T10 all list OTG support — cashify lists "OTG Support, Yes" for the Toughphone and the Toughphone Max, the E10 review lists "USB-C 2.0 (OTG)", and JCB's own T10 page lists "USB-C with OTG support" — but no source I found mentions OTG on the E50. Test with a drive on the E50, and use Method 2 or 4 on that model if the drive never mounts.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — every current JCB model takes a microSD card — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On a JCB Toughphone the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Panasonic Toughbook photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/panasonic-toughbook-photos-to-usb.html

The Toughbook line is mostly Windows laptops — this article is only about the Android handhelds and tablets (FZ-N1, FZ-T1, FZ-S1, FZ-A3, FZ-L1, P-01K), and Panasonic has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the only Toughbook-specific backup advice found is the P-01K FAQ's computer copy or cloud, with no USB-drive route at all. Four honest caveats up front: the original FZ-N1 runs Android 6.0.1, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, so it cannot run SnapDisk at all — only the FZ-N1 mk2, on Android 8.1, can; USB host support is listed only on the FZ-N1 mk2 and the FZ-L1 — Panasonic's own spec sheets list their micro-USB port as "option to be host" — while no source I found mentions host or OTG support on the FZ-T1, the FZ-S1, the FZ-A3, or the P-01K at all, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it; the FZ-S1's microSD support is unconfirmed in the sources I found, so the card is not leaned on for that model; and most search results for this query are not about the Toughbook's own photos at all — they are about using a phone as a bridge to copy a camera's memory card, with "Panasonic" meaning the camera brand, not the device. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On the Android Toughbook models that can run SnapDisk — the FZ-N1 mk2 runs Android 8.1 with a micro-USB port listed as host-capable, the FZ-L1 runs Android 8.1 with the same host-capable listing, the FZ-S1 runs Android 10 with a USB-C port, the FZ-A3 runs Android 9.0 with USB-C, the FZ-T1 runs Android 8.1 with micro-USB, and the P-01K runs Android 8.1 with micro-USB, though host support is unconfirmed on the FZ-T1, the FZ-S1, the FZ-A3, and the P-01K — plug the drive in, then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the generic guides' route is an OTG connection with the built-in file manager — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Panasonic's own file advice works too, but there is none pointing at a USB drive — the P-01K FAQ only offers a computer copy or cloud. Two rival apps do exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, free with ads, a one-time purchase removing the ads; VaultDrive copies photos, videos, and files straight to a USB drive with no computer, free for up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup, Pro $19.99 once — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 18, 2026, no top search result for this query is a Toughbook-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, let alone a Toughbook-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the one Toughbook-specific result is a FAQ page whose backup advice is a computer copy or cloud, and the rest are generic manual guides — most of them about camera memory cards, not the Toughbook's own gallery.

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. Test with a drive on those models, and use Method 2 or 4 on that model if the drive never mounts.; Mistaking a camera-card guide for a Toughbook guide. The PetaPixel and desnoulez guides are real phone-to-USB guides — but they copy a camera's memory card through a hub, with "Panasonic" meaning the camera brand. If your photos are on the Toughbook itself, the card-reader hub is the wrong tool: the drive plugs straight into the Toughbook, and Method 1 or 2 is the route.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the FZ-N1 mk2 and the FZ-L1 take a card up to 64 GB — but the card stays in the device, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the device and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On an Android Toughbook the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the device — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the device. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

Method 3: Method 3: Evolveo's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Evolveo's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Evolveo backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Evolveo StrongPhone Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. Google backup is what Android itself names: personal settings back up to Google's servers with a Google account, and are restored to a new phone when you sign in with that account. It is a real backup — but it backs up settings, not a folder of photo files on a drive you hold. 4. A microSD card is the local option on the G5 and the G9 — both take a card up to 128 GB. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 5. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy DCIM to the computer. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; OTG support is unconfirmed on the G5. The drive mounting is the test.; The Q8 LTE's OTG support is disputed between sources.
