On those phones the computer copy in Method 4 is the route.; The adapter differs by model. The G5 and the G9 have a USB Type-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into either of them and a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter on either of them. The G4, the Q5, and the Q8 LTE have a micro-USB port, so a regular USB-A drive needs a micro-USB OTG adapter on those models. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the G5 and the G9, both of which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter on those models, a micro-USB OTG adapter on the G4, the Q5, and the Q8 LTE. https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/faq.html

The questions a first visitor asks about backing up photos to a USB disk with SnapDisk — answered from how the app actually works in v0.1.2.

TL;DR: SnapDisk backs up your photos to a USB disk — plug it in, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. Nothing is uploaded anywhere: the app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

How does SnapDisk back up my photos? Plug in a USB disk and SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" Tap Backup and your photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The progress notification shows real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, with Pause and Stop. Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice.

How much can I back up for free? The free version backs up photos and videos manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. There is no subscription and no monthly fee — Pro is paid once.

Does SnapDisk upload my photos anywhere? No. Copying runs entirely on your device, from your internal storage to the external disk you choose. The app has no internet permission, so your photos cannot leave your device. It works with the phone in airplane mode — if a backup works in airplane mode, it is offline, and SnapDisk does.

What happens if I unplug the disk mid-copy? The backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the disk is back. A partially copied file resumes from where it stopped instead of starting over, and files that already copied are never copied twice. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup.

What disk formats work? Drives formatted exFAT have no per-file size limit. Drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB — that only matters for very long videos. SnapDisk skips those files, lists them with the reason, and keeps going instead of failing the whole backup. NTFS has not been tested on a real disk yet, so we make no claim about it either way: not supported, not unsupported — untested.

Where do my photos go on the disk? By default SnapDisk copies from /sdcard/DCIM on your phone to /disk/DCIM on the external disk. Both folders can be changed in Settings — open the app and pick your own From and To folders. The app opened is a settings screen only; the backup itself is started from the notification.

Is SnapDisk on Google Play yet? Not yet — the Play listing is being prepared. Until then, install the v0.1.2 APK from the GitHub release page. It needs Android 7.0 or later.

Something does not work. Where do I report it? Open an issue on GitHub — every report gets an answer: github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/issues. If a backup fails, the app shows the full error — copy it into the issue so the cause is visible, not guessed.

A manual, not a guide — and the confirmation that Zebra's own photo advice is a transfer to a host computer, with no USB-drive route at all.; Zebra Android 10 LifeGuard release notes (TC72, TC77, TC52, TC57, TC21, TC26, TC52x, TC57x, MC3300x, MC3300xR, L10A, PS20, TC8300, MC93, VC83, EC30, WT6300, MC2200, MC2700, ET51, ET56 Android 10 10.16.10 LifeGuard Update 97 for NGMS Release Notes ((TC72, TC77, TC52, TC57, TC21, TC26, TC52x, TC57x, MC3300x, MC3300xR, L10A, PS20, TC8300, MC93, VC83, EC30, WT6300, MC2200, MC2700, ET51, ET56 Android 10 10.16.10 LifeGuard Update 97 for NGMS Release Notes))) — Zebra's own release notes: one Android 10 build covering the TC72, TC77, TC52, TC57, TC21, TC26, TC52x, and TC57x. Release notes, not a guide — and the confirmation that the TC72/TC77 and the TC52/TC57 run Android 10 on the current build, so they clear SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum.; Wisesmallbusiness, "Zebra TC21 vs. Zebra TC26 - Review & Comparison" (Zebra TC21 vs. Zebra TC26 - Review & Comparison ((Zebra TC21 vs. Zebra TC26 - Review & Comparison))) — the TC21/TC26 run Android 10, and their predecessors the TC20/TC25 ran Android 7.x Nougat. A review, not a guide — and the confirmation that the TC20/TC25 run Android 7.x, so they clear SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, with no host or OTG mention anywhere in it.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google Drive backs your data up to Google's cloud with 15 GB free, and Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.; None of them is a Zebra-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Zebra photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

Method 3: Method 3: Zebra's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Zebra's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Zebra backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on TC-series handhelds: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. Google backup is what Android itself names: personal settings back up to Google's servers with a Google account, and are restored to a new phone when you sign in with that account. It is a real backup — but it backs up settings, not a folder of photo files on a drive you hold. 4. A microSD card is the local option on the TC52, the TC57, the TC72, and the TC77 — all four take a card up to 256 GB SDXC — and the TC21/TC26 take a microSD card too. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the device, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 5. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the device — the TC52 manual's own route is a photo transfer (PTP) to a host computer, and the TC21-to-PC guide uses a USB-C cable with File transfer (MTP). It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the device. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: A few honest limits, so the automatic copy is not oversold:; Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos..; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them..; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk..; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them..; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the device is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round..; USB host support is unconfirmed on four models. The TC21/TC26, the TC52/TC57, and the TC52x/TC57x list host-capable USB — Zebra's own spec sheets list their USB as "OTG — host/client" or "High Speed (Host and Client)" — but no source I found mentions host or OTG support on the TC72, the TC77, the TC20, or the TC25 at all, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it. The drive mounting is the test..; The connector type is unconfirmed on four models. The TC21, the TC26, the TC52, the TC57, the TC52x, and the TC57x have a USB-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them — but no source I found states the connector type on the TC72, the TC77, the TC20, or the TC25, so check the port on those models before buying an adapter: a regular USB-A drive needs the matching OTG adapter, and a plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter — it connects the device to a computer, which is the opposite direction..; Anything below Android 7.0 cannot run SnapDisk at all. Every model listed here clears the minimum — the TC20/TC25 run Android 7.x, the TC52/TC57 and the TC72/TC77 run Android 8.1, and the TC21/TC26 and the TC52x/TC57x run Android 10 — but older TC-series models exist, so check Settings > About phone if you are unsure: below Android 7.0, SnapDisk cannot install, and the computer copy in Method 4 is the route..; The TC20/TC25's OTG is unconfirmed. The TC20/TC25 run Android 7.x, so they clear SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum — but no source I found mentions host or OTG support on either model, so the drive mounting is the test on those two as well..; "Zebra" also means printers. The top search result for this query is a Zebra printer manual about copying files to a ZT400 printer's flash memory — "Zebra" there means the printer brand, not the handheld. This article is about the photos stored on the TC-series handheld itself..; The adapter differs by model. The TC21, the TC26, the TC52, the TC57, the TC52x, and the TC57x have a USB Type-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them and a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter on any of them. The connector type on the TC72, the TC77, the TC20, and the TC25 is unconfirmed in the sources found, so check the port on those models before buying an adapter. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the device to a computer, which is the opposite direction..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the TC21, the TC26, the TC52, the TC57, the TC52x, and the TC57x, all of which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter on those models. On the TC72, the TC77, the TC20, and the TC25 the connector type is unconfirmed in the sources found, so check the port before buying anything. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the device to a computer, which is the opposite direction..; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your device up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup..; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. A computer copy with a USB cable moves files to a computer — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the device and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy..; Mistaking a spec table or a review page for a phone-to-USB guide. The Zebra spec sheets and the TC21/TC26 review are real Zebra pages — but the spec sheets only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type, and the review only compares the hardware. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the device..; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. The TC21/TC26, the TC52/TC57, and the TC52x/TC57x list host-capable USB — but no source I found mentions host or OTG support on the TC72, the TC77, the TC20, or the TC25. Test with a drive on those models, and use Method 2 or 4 on that model if the drive never mounts..; Mistaking a printer manual for a handheld guide. The Zebra docs result is a real Zebra page — but it copies files to and from a ZT400 industrial printer's flash memory. If your photos are on a TC-series handheld, the printer exercise is the wrong tool: the drive plugs straight into the handheld, and Method 1 or 2 is the route..; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the TC52, the TC57, the TC72, and the TC77 take a card up to 256 GB SDXC, and the TC21/TC26 take a microSD card too — but the card stays in the device, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is..; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the device and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026..; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On a TC-series handheld the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost..; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the device — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check..; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the device. Copy first, verify, then delete..; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..


### Back up Honeywell photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/honeywell-photos-to-usb.html

The CT-series is Honeywell's line of enterprise Android handhelds (CT30 XP, CT40, CT45, CT47, CT60), and Honeywell has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the only Honeywell-specific backup advice found is the CT60 and EDA51 manuals' file sync to a host computer, with no USB-drive route at all. Four honest caveats up front: USB OTG support is listed only on the CT45 and the CT47 — Honeywell's own datasheets say "USB OTG supported via I/O ports" — while no source I found mentions host or OTG support on the CT30 XP, the CT40, or the CT60 at all, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it; every model listed clears SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum — the CT40 and the CT60 run Android 7.1, upgradable to Android 11, the CT30 XP and the CT45 run Android 11 to 13, and the CT47 runs Android 12 to 16 — but the older CT50 runs Android 6.0 and cannot run SnapDisk at all; all five models have a USB-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them; and "Honeywell" also means DVRs and USB drives — the top search result for this query is a Honeywell DVR manual about archiving video to a USB stick, not photos off a handheld. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On the CT-series models that can run SnapDisk — the CT45 runs Android 11 to 13 and the CT47 runs Android 12 to 16, and Honeywell's own datasheets list USB OTG support on both; the CT30 XP runs Android 11 to 13, the CT40 and the CT60 run Android 7.1, upgradable to Android 11, all three with a USB-C port, though host or OTG support is unconfirmed on all three — plug the drive in, then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the generic guides' route is an OTG connection with the built-in file manager — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Honeywell's own file advice works too, but there is none pointing at a USB drive — the CT60 manual only offers a file sync to a host computer. Two rival apps do exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, free with ads, a one-time purchase removing the ads; VaultDrive copies photos, videos, and files straight to a USB drive with no computer, free for up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup, Pro $19.99 once — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the handheld afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 18, 2026, no top search result for this query is a Honeywell-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, let alone a Honeywell-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the two Honeywell-specific results are guides to connecting a CT60 to a PC, and the top result is a DVR manual, not a handheld guide at all.

Search "back up Honeywell photos to USB drive without computer" and there is no Honeywell-specific phone-to-USB guide in the top results at all — the two Honeywell-specific results are guides to connecting a CT60 to a PC, and the top result is a Honeywell DVR manual about archiving video from an HRDE4X4 DVR to a USB stick, not photos off a handheld. Honeywell has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own; the CT60 manual's only file advice is a sync to a host computer (MTP/PTP). USB OTG support is listed only on the CT45 and the CT47 (Honeywell's own datasheets say "USB OTG supported via I/O ports"); host or OTG support is unconfirmed on the CT30 XP, the CT40, and the CT60 — the drive mounting is the test on those models. The CT40 and the CT60 run Android 7.1, upgradable to Android 11; the CT30 XP and the CT45 run Android 11 to 13; the CT47 runs Android 12 to 16; the older CT50 runs Android 6.0 and cannot run SnapDisk at all. All five models have a USB-C port. Google Photos and Google Drive compared, plus Files by Google manual copy; original files, byte-for-byte copy, size-checked.
